title: FaST: Efficient and Effective Long-Horizon Forecasting for Large-Scale Spatial-Temporal Graphs via Mixture-of-Experts

problem.claim: Large-scale spatial-temporal graph forecasting requires long-horizon predictions over large networks.

gap.claim: Existing models mainly target short horizons and incur substantial computational and memory costs when extended to long horizons and large graphs.

contributions.claim: FaST is an effective and efficient heterogeneity-aware Mixture-of-Experts framework for long-horizon, large-scale spatial-temporal graph forecasting.
FaST introduces an adaptive graph agent attention mechanism to reduce the computational burden of conventional graph convolution and self-attention on large graphs.
FaST introduces a parallel Mixture-of-Experts module that replaces traditional feed-forward networks with Gated Linear Units to provide an efficient, scalable parallel structure.

author_reported_evidence.claim: On real-world datasets, the authors report superior long-horizon predictive accuracy compared with state-of-the-art baselines.
On real-world datasets, the authors report remarkable computational efficiency compared with state-of-the-art baselines.
The authors report that source code is publicly available.

narrative_sequence.summary: Spatial-temporal graph forecasting on large-scale networks is an active research area.
Existing approaches focus mainly on short horizons and scale poorly in computation and memory for long-horizon forecasting on large graphs.
FaST addresses these challenges with a heterogeneity-aware Mixture-of-Experts framework supporting one-week-ahead forecasting at 672 fifteen-minute steps with thousands of nodes.
The framework uses adaptive graph agent attention and a parallel Mixture-of-Experts module based on Gated Linear Units.
Experiments on real-world datasets are reported to show improved predictive accuracy and computational efficiency over state-of-the-art baselines.

source_observation.claim: The framework combines a mechanism for reducing graph-processing cost with a parallel expert architecture for scalable sequence modeling.

interpretation.claim: Scaling long-horizon forecasting may require reducing both graph-interaction complexity and feed-forward computation.

application.claim: For other large graph forecasting problems, consider jointly addressing graph-operation cost and model-block parallelism.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this combination benefits graph forecasting tasks beyond the reported setting.

unknowns: Specific datasets, baselines, metrics, and quantitative results are not provided.
The abstract does not describe model training details, resource usage, ablations, or limitations.
